sourcingNote:
This section goes further than the other culture topics: it is also about how people in France live, talk and behave, not only about rules.
So it has its own rule. A statement about people either rests on a statistic or an official source, or it is marked as common practice. Under a topic you find the sources and the date they are from. Where a topic has no source list, it describes common practice: it is not a survey result, and it varies by person, age and region. We write "many" or "most", never "the French are ...". About 68 million people live in France (INSEE, 2026, check the current figure), and they are all different: young and old, from Brittany to Corsica, from big cities and from villages, born in France or abroad.
Where something is debated, both sides are shown. Rules and figures change; if in doubt, the linked official source is right.

topics.title: Saying hello: bonjour first, la bise, handshake
topics.intro: In France, the first thing many people do is say “Bonjour”, in a shop, a waiting room or a lift, before any question. Friends and family often greet each other with la bise (light kisses on the cheeks). At work, a handshake is normal when you meet someone for the first time.
topics.question: Comment est-ce qu’on se salue dans votre pays ? (How do people greet each other in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the age, the region and the place.

“Bonjour” comes before everything else. If you start with a question and forget the greeting, some people feel you skipped a step. In a shop, say “Bonjour, Madame” or “Bonjour, Monsieur” when you come in.

La bise: light cheek-to-cheek kisses, with a kissing sound but usually without a real kiss. It is common between friends and family. The number (often two, sometimes more) depends on the region, so watch the other person.

At work, many people shake hands at a first meeting and say “Enchanté” or “Enchantée”. With colleagues you see every day, habits depend on the company: some do la bise, some shake hands, some only say hello.
When you leave a shop or a doctor’s waiting room, many people say “Au revoir” and add “Bonne journée” (or “Bonne soirée” in the evening). After about six in the evening, “Bonsoir” replaces “Bonjour”.
In Québec, “bonjour” is also used to say goodbye, and “allô” can be a casual hello.
topics.context: If you are not sure, wait for the other person. If they lean in for la bise, do the same. If they put out a hand, shake it. Nobody will mind a small mistake, but a missing “Bonjour” is noticed more than a wrong kiss.
phrases: Bonjour, enchanté. (Hello, nice to meet you. A woman says “enchantée”.)
Bonjour, Madame ! (Hello! Said when you come into a shop.)
Ça va ? (How are you?)
Ça va bien, merci. Et vous ? (Fine, thanks. And you?)
Bonjour à tous. (Good morning, everybody.)
Merci, au revoir, bonne journée. (Thank you, goodbye, have a good day.)

quiz.prompt: You meet your new boss for the first time. What do most people do?
quiz.answer: Shake hands
quiz.explain: A handshake is normal at a first meeting at work. Wait and see if the other person suggests something else.

quiz.prompt: You enter a small shop. What do you say first?
quiz.answer: Bonjour.
quiz.explain: “Bonjour” comes first, before you ask for anything. “Au revoir” is for leaving.

quiz.prompt: What is la bise?
options: Light kisses on the cheeks, often two
quiz.answer: Light kisses on the cheeks, often two
quiz.explain: La bise is a common greeting between friends and family. The number of kisses depends on the region.

topics.title: Queues and personal space
topics.intro: In France, people usually wait in order in shops, at the market and at the doctor, but the line is not always clear. You ask who is last, and then you know your turn. In a lift or on the métro, strangers usually keep their distance and say little.
topics.question: Comment fait-on la queue dans votre pays ? (How do people queue in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the place and the situation.

In a bakery, a market or a waiting room with no clear line, people often ask “C’est qui, le dernier ?” or “Qui est le dernier ?” (Who is last?). Someone answers “C’est moi”, and after that you know who is before you.
At a counter, if someone goes in front of you, a polite and clear phrase is “Excusez-moi, je crois que j’étais avant vous.”
Friends and family are close when they greet each other, but many strangers keep some distance and do not talk in public transport. It is neutral, not cold.
If you touch someone by accident, say “Pardon”. To pass, say “Excusez-moi, je peux passer ?”
topics.context: At the préfecture, the CAF or a hospital there is often a ticket machine or a numbered system. If not, ask who is last when you arrive, and say “C’est moi” to the next person.
phrases: Qui est le dernier ? (Who is last?)
C’est moi. (It is me. Said by the last person.)
Excusez-moi, je peux passer ? (Excuse me, can I get past?)
Pardon. (Sorry.)
Excusez-moi, je crois que j’étais avant vous. (Excuse me, I think I was before you.)

quiz.prompt: You enter a bakery with no clear line. What do you ask?
quiz.answer: Qui est le dernier ?
quiz.explain: You ask who is last, then you know when it is your turn.

quiz.prompt: Someone goes in front of you at a counter. Which phrase is polite and clear?
options: Excusez-moi, je crois que j’étais avant vous.
quiz.answer: Excusez-moi, je crois que j’étais avant vous.
quiz.explain: It says what you think without an accusation.

quiz.prompt: You push past someone by accident. What do you say?
quiz.answer: Pardon.
quiz.explain: “Pardon” or “Excusez-moi” is the normal word for a small mistake.

topics.title: Please and thank you, tu and vous
topics.intro: In France, politeness sits in small words: bonjour, s’il vous plaît, merci, Madame, Monsieur. A bare “Un café !” can sound curt, but “Bonjour, je voudrais un café, s’il vous plaît” is just normal. Choosing between tu and vous is part of it too.
topics.question: Comment demandez-vous les choses dans votre pays ? (How do you ask for things in your country?)

table.label: What you say, and what it does
rows: Bonjour, je voudrais un café, s’il vous plaît.
A normal, polite order in a café or shop. “Je voudrais” is softer than “Je veux”.
Excusez-moi. / Pardon.
Gets someone’s attention, or says sorry for a small thing. “Excusez-moi” is a bit more formal.
Merci, c’est gentil.
Thank you, that is kind. People say thanks often: when they pay, get something and leave.
Vous / tu
Use “vous” with strangers, older people and in formal situations. “Tu” is for friends, family, children and many young people.
On peut se tutoyer ?
A polite way to suggest “tu”. Usually the older person or the one with more power proposes it.
Bonne journée. / Bonne soirée.
A friendly goodbye after a short contact, in a shop, at a counter or in the lift.

facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the age, the region and the situation.
In a shop or a café, many people start with “Bonjour”, ask with “Je voudrais…” or “Je vais prendre…” and finish with “Merci” and “Au revoir”. A request with only a noun can sound curt.
Use “vous” with strangers, with older people and in formal contexts (administration, a boss you do not know). Among friends, family, children and in many young teams, “tu” is normal.
If someone uses “vous” with you, using “tu” back can sound rude. If you are unsure, start with “vous” and wait for a suggestion.
“Madame” and “Monsieur” are used a lot with strangers: “Merci, Madame.” In administration, “Mademoiselle” was removed from official forms in 2012, and “Madame” is the normal word for an adult woman.
topics.context: If a native speaker sounds short, it is not always anger. Listen to the tone and the greeting. A smile and “merci” make a short sentence warm.
phrases: Bonjour, je voudrais un café, s’il vous plaît. (Hello, I would like a coffee, please.)
Je vais prendre un café crème. (I will have a coffee with milk.)
Excusez-moi, vous avez l’heure ? (Excuse me, do you have the time?)
Très bien, parfait, merci. (Very good, perfect, thanks.)
Merci beaucoup, bonne journée. (Thank you very much, have a good day.)
On peut se tutoyer ? (Can we use “tu”?)

quiz.prompt: Which is the polite way to order a coffee in a café?
options: Bonjour, je voudrais un café, s’il vous plaît.
quiz.answer: Bonjour, je voudrais un café, s’il vous plaît.
quiz.explain: A greeting, “je voudrais” and “s’il vous plaît” make it polite and warm.

quiz.prompt: What does “On peut se tutoyer ?” mean?
options: Can we use “tu” with each other?
quiz.answer: Can we use “tu” with each other?
quiz.explain: It is a polite way to move from “vous” to “tu”.

quiz.prompt: You want to pass a person in a crowded place. Which phrase fits?
quiz.answer: Excusez-moi.
quiz.explain: “Excusez-moi” means excuse me. “Bon appétit” is for someone who eats.

topics.title: Time, lunch breaks and strikes
topics.intro: In France, lunch is a real break for many people, and dinner is usually not before about 19:30 or 20:00. A little lateness at a dinner with friends is common. At the préfecture, at a job interview and at the doctor, people expect you on time. Strikes (grèves) can also change your day, so check the news.
topics.question: Que se passe-t-il si vous arrivez en retard dans votre pays ? (What happens if you are late in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the region, the age and the situation.

Many people have lunch (le déjeuner) between about 12:00 and 14:00, and many workplaces have a lunch break (la pause déjeuner) of about an hour. Many restaurants serve lunch only in this time. Dinner (le dîner) is often around 19:30 to 21:00.

For a dinner at someone’s home, arriving about ten minutes after the time given is common. For a drink or a party, a little more is accepted. If you are much later, send a message: “J’arrive dans dix minutes.”

At the préfecture, at the doctor’s, for a job interview and at work, be on time or a bit early. A booked appointment (un rendez-vous) means a fixed time, and many offices can refuse you if you are late.
“Tout à l’heure” can mean “in a little while” or “a little while ago”. The verb tense shows which one. “À tout à l’heure” means “see you in a bit”. If a time is important, ask for an hour.

A grève (strike) is part of public life in France. Rail, métro, schools and other services can be affected, often with a notice (préavis) some days before. Check the website or app of your operator, and leave early on a strike day.
topics.context: If you are late, say so early and say why in a short sentence. A short message is better than silence. On days with strikes, the usual advice is to look at the news and the operator’s page the evening before.
phrases: On se dit quelle heure ? (What time shall we say?)
J’arrive dans dix minutes. (I will be there in ten minutes.)
Excusez-moi pour le retard. (Sorry for being late.)
J’ai rendez-vous à dix heures. (I have an appointment at ten.)
À quelle heure, exactement ? (At what time, exactly?)
Il y a une grève demain, les trains sont perturbés. (There is a strike tomorrow, the trains are disrupted.)

quiz.prompt: You have a préfecture appointment at ten. When do you arrive?
options: At ten, or a bit before
quiz.answer: At ten, or a bit before
quiz.explain: At the préfecture, the doctor and at work, people usually expect you on time.

quiz.prompt: A friend invites you to dinner at 20:00. What is common?
quiz.answer: Arrive about ten minutes later
quiz.explain: A short delay at a private dinner is common. If it is more, send a message.

quiz.prompt: What is a grève?
quiz.answer: A strike
quiz.explain: Strikes can disrupt trains, métro and schools. Check the operator’s page.

topics.title: Paying the bill
topics.intro: In France, friends often take turns to pay, and one person may say “C’est ma tournée” (my round) or “Je t’invite” (my treat). Splitting the bill equally is also common. A friendly argument about who pays is normal.
topics.question: Qui paie dans votre pays quand on sort en groupe ? (Who pays in your country when people go out together?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the group, the age and the place.
“Inviter” means to pay for the others. “Je t’invite” means it is my treat. Next time, someone else pays: “Cette fois, c’est moi” or “C’est ma tournée”.

“On partage ?” or “On fait moitié-moitié” means to split equally. “Chacun sa part” means everybody pays for their own food and drink. In a big group of friends, some people say “On fait un pot commun” (we put money in a shared pot) for a trip or a gift.
Offering to pay once or twice is normal. People say “Non, non, je t’invite” and the other person says “Allez, c’est pour moi”. After that, you can accept and say thanks.

In a restaurant, you ask for the bill with “L’addition, s’il vous plaît”. The waiter does not always bring it without being asked. Prices usually include service, so a tip is optional. For paying separately, ask “On peut payer séparément ?”. It depends on the place. Many people also send their share by bank transfer (un virement) or an app.
topics.context: If you do not want to pay for others, say it early and clearly: “Moi, je paie ce que j’ai pris.” Most people understand this.
phrases: L’addition, s’il vous plaît. (The bill, please.)
Je t’invite. (It is my treat.)
On partage ? (Shall we split it?)
Je te fais un virement ce soir. (I will send you the money by transfer tonight.)
Cette fois, c’est moi. (This time it is me.)
Chacun sa part. (Everybody pays their own share.)

quiz.prompt: A friend says “Je t’invite.” What does that mean?
quiz.answer: I pay for you
quiz.explain: “Inviter” in this situation means to pay for the others.

quiz.prompt: What does “Chacun sa part” mean?
quiz.answer: Everybody pays their own share
quiz.explain: Each person pays for what they had, or an equal part.

quiz.prompt: What is “un pot commun” among friends?
options: Money that everybody puts together for something
quiz.answer: Money that everybody puts together for something
quiz.explain: People use it for a gift, a trip or shared costs.

topics.title: Small talk and l’apéro
topics.intro: In France, many people meet and talk at l’apéro, a drink with small snacks before a meal, often at home or in a café. Small talk is easy with food, holidays, the region and work. Many people also like a good debate about politics, and a shared râler (a good grumble) about transport or taxes can feel friendly.
topics.question: De quoi parle-t-on avec des gens qu’on vient de rencontrer dans votre pays ? (What do people talk about with new people in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the group, the age and the place.

L’apéro (l’apéritif) is a drink and a few snacks, such as crisps, olives or sausage, before lunch or dinner. “Passez prendre l’apéro” is an easy invitation. An “apéro dînatoire” has so much food that it replaces dinner.
Safe topics for a first talk: food, where you are from, holidays, work, family, the region you live in, the weather, and sport.

Many people discuss politics with friends and enjoy strong opinions. It does not always mean a quarrel. With new people, listen first. Questions about salary and money are usually too personal at first.

“Râler” means to grumble or complain. Many people râler about trains, the weather, bureaucracy or taxes, and it can be a way to bond. If you criticise France yourself, some people react differently, so follow their lead.
topics.context: People may ask questions that feel personal, for example what you do for a living. Usually it is interest, not a test. You can answer short or say “Je préfère ne pas en parler.”
phrases: Tu viens prendre l’apéro samedi ? (Are you coming for an apéro on Saturday?)
Tu es d’où ? (Where are you from?)
Et vous, vous faites quoi dans la vie ? (And you, what do you do?)
Ça fait un an que j’habite en France. (I have lived in France for a year.)
Ah là là, ces transports, c’est pénible ! (Oh dear, these trains and buses, it is so annoying!)
Je préfère ne pas en parler. (I prefer not to talk about it.)

quiz.prompt: What is l’apéro?
options: A drink with snacks before a meal
quiz.answer: A drink with snacks before a meal
quiz.explain: People meet for a drink and small snacks before lunch or dinner.

quiz.prompt: Which topic is usually safe for a first talk?
quiz.answer: Food and holidays
quiz.explain: Food, holidays and the region are easy topics. Salary is more personal.

quiz.prompt: What does “râler” mean?
quiz.answer: To grumble or complain
quiz.explain: It is a common, often friendly, way to talk about annoying things.

topics.title: Making friends
topics.intro: In France, friendships often start in small circles: a club (association), a language exchange, work, the school gate or the building. You often meet people in a WhatsApp group first, then at an apéro. It takes time, but small steps help.
topics.question: Où rencontre-t-on de nouvelles personnes dans votre pays ? (Where do people meet new people in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the city, the age and the person.

Many buildings have a WhatsApp group for neighbours. It is useful for news, noise and small problems. Say hello in it and keep your messages short. The Fête des voisins (neighbours’ party) is usually held at the end of May, and many buildings and streets join in.

In a building with owners, the copropriété is the group of owners. They meet once a year at an assemblée générale about costs and repairs, with a manager called le syndic. Tenants usually do not vote, but the landlord does.
An association (under the law of 1901) is a non-profit group, for example a sports club, a choir, a language café or a volunteer group. Many people meet friends this way.
At work, a “pot” (a drink and snacks) marks a welcome, a farewell or a birthday. At the school gate, parents often have a WhatsApp group for their class.
topics.context: Plans in France often start with “On se fait un truc un de ces quatre”. Say a day: “Samedi, ça vous dit ?” A concrete offer makes a friendship start.
phrases: Je suis votre nouveau voisin du troisième. (I am your new neighbour from the third floor.)
Il y a un groupe WhatsApp pour l’immeuble ? (Is there a WhatsApp group for the building?)
On se voit samedi ? (Shall we meet on Saturday?)
Je cherche un tandem pour parler français. (I am looking for a language exchange partner to speak French.)
Comment je peux m’inscrire à l’association ? (How can I join the association?)
Vous voulez venir prendre un café ? (Would you like to come for a coffee?)

quiz.prompt: What is an association (law of 1901)?
options: A non-profit group, for example a club
quiz.answer: A non-profit group, for example a club
quiz.explain: Sports clubs, choirs and volunteer groups are often associations.

quiz.prompt: What is the copropriété?
options: The group of owners in a building
quiz.answer: The group of owners in a building
quiz.explain: It decides about costs and repairs in the building.

quiz.prompt: You want to turn “On se fait un truc un de ces quatre” into a plan. What helps?
quiz.answer: Say a day
quiz.explain: A concrete offer, for example “Samedi, ça vous dit ?”, makes the plan real.

topics.title: How hiring works
topics.intro: In France, employers look at your CV, and many also use their own contacts. A photo on the CV is optional. Job sites, personal networks and the public employment service (France Travail) all play a part.
topics.question: Comment cherche-t-on du travail dans votre pays ? (How do people look for work in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the sector, the company, the region and the age of the applicant.

France Travail is the public employment service (the former Pôle emploi). It offers vacancies and support. Many people also use job sites such as LinkedIn or Indeed and temp agencies (intérim). Check francetravail.fr for the current offer.
A CV is often one or two pages. A photo is optional, and many advice sites say you can leave it out. A cover letter (lettre de motivation) is still asked for in many applications.
Personal contacts count. Getting a job through a contact can be called “le piston”, a word often used critically, but asking people you know for tips (“le réseau”) is normal.

Common contracts are the CDI (open-ended), the CDD (fixed-term) and intérim. A trial period (période d’essai) is common, and its length depends on the law, the type of contract and the convention collective (the sector agreement). Read your contract and ask.

pros: A personal contact can open a door, and a tip from a friend is quick.
A short CV is easy to read and compare.
Many employers call you early on, so things can move fast.
cons: People without a network in France can feel left out.
A name, an address or an age can influence some employers, although the law forbids discrimination.
The trial period and the type of contract can be unclear if you do not read the contract.

topics.context: Tell people you know that you are looking for work. Many vacancies are found by word of mouth, and you can still apply on the job sites in parallel.
phrases: Je cherche un poste dans la restauration. (I am looking for a job in catering.)
Je vous envoie mon CV et ma lettre de motivation. (I am sending you my CV and my cover letter.)
Quelle est la durée de la période d’essai ? (How long is the trial period?)
Quelle convention collective s’applique ? (Which collective agreement applies?)
J’ai travaillé trois ans dans un magasin. (I worked for three years in a shop.)
Je peux commencer lundi, si vous voulez. (I can start on Monday, if you like.)

quiz.prompt: What is “le piston” in the context of hiring?
options: A job through a personal contact
quiz.answer: A job through a personal contact
quiz.explain: The word is often used critically, but asking people you know for tips is normal.

quiz.prompt: Where can you find the length of a trial period?
options: In the law, the convention collective and your contract
quiz.answer: In the law, the convention collective and your contract
quiz.explain: The length depends on the type of contract, the law and the sector agreement. Read your contract and ask.

quiz.prompt: Is a photo on the CV required in France?
quiz.answer: No, it is optional
quiz.explain: A photo is not required, and many people leave it out.

topics.title: Cars, driving licence and getting around
topics.intro: In France, how you travel depends on where you live: in big cities many people use the métro, the bus, the RER or the tram, and between cities the TGV is popular. In small towns and villages, a car is often needed. Speed limits, the alcohol limit and the points on the driving licence (permis à points) are part of daily life for drivers.
topics.question: Comment vous déplacez-vous dans votre ville ? (How do you get around in your city?)
facts: The SNCF runs the TGV (high-speed trains between big cities), the TER (regional trains) and many commuter lines. In Paris and its region the RER, the métro and the Transilien trains are used a lot.

On motorways (autoroutes) the general limit for cars is 130 km/h, and 110 km/h in rain. On other roads outside towns the usual limit is 80 km/h or 90 km/h, depending on the road. Signs show the real limit, so always read them.
In towns, the general limit is 50 km/h, and many towns have 30 km/h zones. Signs and the town hall decide.
The general blood alcohol limit for drivers is 0.5 g/l. It is lower (0.2 g/l) for drivers with a probationary licence (permis probatoire). Check service-public.fr for the current rules.

The contrôle technique is the regular technical check for a car. It is usually due after four years and then every two years. Many cities also have zones à faibles émissions (low-emission zones), and a Crit’Air sticker shows your car’s category.

A driving licence from another country: whether you can use it or must exchange it depends on the country, and there can be a deadline after you start living in France. Check service-public.fr for your licence.

prosCons.prosLabel: Why many people like the car
pros: It is flexible for villages, shift work and trips with children.
In many regions, public transport is rare outside the big towns.
It saves time on routes without a direct train.
prosCons.consLabel: Why many people prefer public transport
cons: Parking, fuel, tolls and low-emission zones cost time and money.
In cities, the métro, the bus and the RER are often faster at rush hour.
A train lets you read or work on the way.

topics.context: If you plan to drive, check three things early: your licence, the insurance and the Crit’Air sticker if you enter a big city. Ask on service-public.fr or at the préfecture.
phrases: Comment je vais à la gare ? (How do I get to the station?)
Un billet aller-retour pour Lyon, s’il vous plaît. (A return ticket to Lyon, please.)
Où est-ce que je peux me garer par ici ? (Where can I park around here?)
Ma voiture a passé le contrôle technique. (My car has passed the contrôle technique.)
Je peux échanger mon permis de conduire ? (Can I exchange my driving licence?)
Je n’ai rien bu, c’est moi qui conduis. (I have not drunk anything, I am driving.)

sources.label: Service-public.fr: driving licence, road rules and exchanging a foreign licence (search the topic “permis de conduire”)
sources.stand: check the current version on the site

quiz.prompt: What is the general limit for cars on a motorway in dry weather?
quiz.answer: 130 km/h
quiz.explain: It is 130 km/h in dry weather and 110 km/h in rain, unless signs say otherwise.

quiz.prompt: What is the contrôle technique?
options: The regular technical check for a car
quiz.answer: The regular technical check for a car
quiz.explain: It is a compulsory check of the car’s condition, at fixed intervals.

quiz.prompt: Can you always use a foreign licence in France?
options: It depends on the country of the licence
quiz.answer: It depends on the country of the licence
quiz.explain: Whether you can use it or must exchange it depends on the country. Check service-public.fr.

topics.title: Women and men at work
topics.intro: In France, the law requires equal pay for equal work or work of equal value, and large companies must publish an equality score. A pay gap between women and men still shows in the statistics. Many people debate how to close it and how much comes from part-time work and care duties.
topics.question: Comment se partagent le travail et les soins aux enfants dans votre pays ? (How are work and care shared in your country?)
facts: French labour law requires equal pay for equal work or for work of equal value. It also forbids discrimination in hiring and at work.
Companies with 50 or more employees publish a yearly score, the Index de l’égalité professionnelle, out of 100. Ask your human resources department (RH) or your CSE about your company’s score.

INSEE publishes figures on pay gaps. In recent years the gap in average pay between women and men has been roughly 14 to 15 % in the private sector for full-time equivalents, and larger for total earnings. Check the latest edition on insee.fr.
Part-time work is more common among women, according to labour statistics, and this is one reason often given for the gap. Experts discuss how large the other parts are.

Both parents can take leave after a birth: a maternity leave for the mother and a leave for the second parent, extended in 2021 to about four weeks, partly compulsory. Further changes have been announced, so check service-public.fr.

Since 2022, parents can choose the surname of a child: the father’s, the mother’s, or both in the order they choose. A person’s legal name is the birth name. Married people may use their spouse’s name as a nom d’usage.

prosCons.prosLabel: What many people point to as progress
pros: A public score for companies makes the debate more factual.
Leave for both parents supports shared care.
Parents can now choose the child’s surname.
prosCons.consLabel: What many people say is still open
cons: The gap in average earnings remains.
Care work still falls more often on women.
People disagree about the reasons and about the best measures.

topics.context: If you are an employee and have a question about leave or pay, ask the human resources department (RH), your union representative, the CSE or the Sécurité sociale. Do not rely on the opinion of a colleague alone.
phrases: Je voudrais poser mon congé de paternité. (I would like to take my paternity leave.)
Ma femme et moi, on se partage les tâches. (My wife and I share the tasks.)
Mon nom de naissance est Martin. (My birth name is Martin.)
C’est un temps partiel à quel pourcentage ? (What percentage is the part-time job?)

topics.title: Dating basics
topics.intro: In France, people often start with a simple plan: prendre un verre (have a drink) or dîner (have dinner). Many adults meet through friends, work, hobbies or dating apps. Be clear, be respectful, and listen to the other person’s answer.
topics.question: Comment propose-t-on un premier rendez-vous dans votre pays ? (How do people suggest a first date in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It varies by person, age, region and city.
“Tu es libre samedi soir ?” or “On prend un verre ?” is a relaxed invitation to a drink, and it is an easy first plan. “Draguer” means to flirt or chat someone up.
Many adults use dating apps such as Tinder, Bumble or Hinge, but also meet through friends, at work or in clubs.
Who pays varies. Some people split, some take turns, and sometimes one person invites the first time. Say what you prefer in a friendly way: “On partage ?” or “Je t’invite.”

On a first date, people often greet each other with la bise. “Tu” is usual between people of the same age. Meeting friends or family usually comes later. “Non” or “Ça ne me dit rien” is a full answer, and it should be respected.
topics.context: Be honest and clear about what you want. If you do not want a second date, you can say it kindly: “J’ai passé un très bon moment, mais je ne pense pas que ce soit ce que je cherche.”

J’aimerais te présenter mes amis. (I would like to introduce you to my friends.)
Merci pour la soirée, mais je ne cherche rien de sérieux. (Thanks for the evening, but I am not looking for anything serious.)

topics.title: Direct and indirect
topics.intro: In France, some everyday phrases are softer, or stronger, than they sound. “On verra” is often a gentle no or “not yet”, and “C’est pas mal” can be real praise. At the same time, many people enjoy open debate, and a plain “non, merci” is normal and not rude.
topics.question: Comment dites-vous non sans offenser ? (How do you say no without offending?)

table.label: What is said, and what it can mean
rows: On verra.
Often “I will decide later”, and sometimes a soft no. Ask for a day.
On s’appelle ! / On se fait un truc un de ces quatre.
A friendly wish to meet, without a fixed plan. Suggest a day if you want to meet.
C’est pas mal.
Often real praise, “quite good”, said in a casual way. The tone and the face show how warm it is.
Oui, mais…
A polite start to disagree or to correct, as in “Oui, mais je ne suis pas sûr…”.
Ce n’est pas évident.
It is not easy. It can be a soft way to say it is difficult or not possible.
Non, merci.
A clear and polite no, for example when the waiter offers dessert. It is not rude.

facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the region, the age and the relationship.
In a café or a shop, a plain “non, merci” is normal and not rude. You do not need a long excuse.
Debate is a social pastime for many people. Among friends and colleagues, disagreeing, interrupting and strong opinions are often a sign of interest in the topic, not of anger.
At work, criticism is often softened: “Il faudrait peut-être revoir ça” (maybe we should look at this again) can mean “this must change”. Listen to the tone and ask a follow-up question.
If you are not sure what a phrase means, ask in a friendly way: “Alors, on se voit jeudi ?”
topics.context: Style varies a lot by region and person. If a phrase is unclear, repeat it in your own words, or suggest a concrete day. This is clearer for both sides and is not rude.
phrases: On verra, je te dis ça demain. (We will see, I will tell you tomorrow.)
On s’appelle un de ces jours ! (Let’s call each other one of these days!)
Oui, mais je ne suis pas sûr que ce soit une bonne idée. (Yes, but I am not sure it is a good idea.)
Ce n’est pas évident, mais je vais essayer. (It is not easy, but I will try.)
Alors, on se voit jeudi, oui ou non ? (So, are we meeting on Thursday, yes or no?)
Non, merci, ça ira. (No, thanks, I am fine.)

topics.title: Humour and banter
topics.intro: In France, many people use humour to build closeness: chambrer (to tease in fun), irony and the second degree (humour that is not meant literally) are common among friends and colleagues. Jokes about regions and accents also exist, so listen first and join in only when you know the people. Political satire, such as the weekly Le Canard enchaîné, has a long tradition.
topics.question: Avec qui plaisantez-vous, et avec qui non ? (Who do you joke with and who not?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the group, the age and the situation.
“Chambrer” (informal) means to tease someone in fun. “Je plaisante” or “Je rigole” tells people it was not serious. “C’était pour rire” means it was only for fun.
Irony is common, often at the second degree: someone may say “Super, merci…” when something is bad. Tone and face show it. “Tu l’as pris au premier degré ?” asks if you took it literally.

Jokes about regions or accents, for example about people from the north, the south or Paris, are often heard. They are not welcome in every case. If you are new, do not start them. Wait until you know the people.
Le Canard enchaîné is a satirical weekly newspaper that has existed since 1915, and press cartoons (dessins de presse) are a long tradition. People debate where the limits of humour lie.

pros: Teasing between friends is a sign of trust.
Irony makes difficult things easier to say.
Satire and cartoons are a long public tradition.
cons: A joke that works in one group may hurt in another.
As a newcomer, you may not know the limits yet.
Jokes about origin, religion or looks can hurt, even if the speaker means well.

topics.context: Join the banter with a small, kind joke about yourself first, such as your French mistakes. If someone looks upset, say “C’était pour rire, excuse-moi.”

Mon français est un désastre, mais j’essaie. (My French is a disaster, but I am trying.)
